item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q001_histone_related_proteins","answer":"Proteins related to core histones in SCOPe are the histone-fold proteins. SCOPe places the histone fold in class a, all-alpha proteins; fold a.22, Histone-fold; and superfamily a.22.1, Histone-fold. Eukaryotic core histones H2A, H2B, H3, H4 and close variants such as CENP-A are the closest relatives and should be treated at the family level within the histone-fold superfamily. More distant relatives include archaeal histones and histone-fold transcription-factor subunits such as TAF/TAFII histone-fold pairs, NF-YB/NF-YC, and NC2/Dr1-DRAP1-like proteins: these share the same SCOPe fold and superfamily but are separate families, so the relationship is remote homology through the histone-fold dimerization/DNA-binding architecture rather than interchangeable histone function. Proteins often called histone-like, such as bacterial HU/IHF or linker histone H1, should not automatically be grouped with core histones: H1 is mainly a winged-helix linker histone, and bacterial HU/IHF are histone-like by DNA-packaging role/name, not by SCOPe a.22 histone-fold family membership. Thus template use or function transfer is strongest among same-family core histones, more limited across different a.22.1 families, and unsafe for proteins sharing only a generic DNA-binding or chromatin-associated role.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
